note: How an engagement is actually shaped. The opportunity itself is generated from what Lyzr has delivered; these are the commitments underneath it, and a model never writes them. {unit} is the one thing the pilot runs on, supplied per line and capped at four words: one approval chain, one hiring flow, one business unit.

patterns.when: The client already runs the process and the partner already works inside it. The question is which part of it stops being manual first.

first_offer.name: {work} assessment
first_offer.ends_with: the process mapped end to end with the manual steps costed, and a scoped pilot on one of them

delivery.shape: 8 to 10 week build on one {unit}, then a managed fee to run and extend it

patterns.expansion: A monthly fee to run it, then the same pattern on the next {unit} in the same account
discovery: How many {unit}s run this process, and how often
Which steps are already rule-based, and which need judgement
Which systems hold the data the steps read
Who approves an exception today, and how it reaches them

roles.partner: The process knowledge, the client relationship, the integration and the delivery team
roles.lyzr: The platform the agents run on, the controls, and support through the first build

patterns.when: The work is technically uncertain rather than commercially uncertain. Prove it on one narrow case, then sell the rollout.

first_offer.name: {work} feasibility proof
first_offer.ends_with: a working proof on one {unit}, with the accuracy measured against their own examples

delivery.shape: 6 week proof on one {unit}, then a per-{unit} rollout
delivery.team_needed: 1 engineer + 1 person from the client who knows the exceptions

patterns.expansion: Each further {unit} is a shorter build on the same proven pattern
discovery: How many {unit}s exist, and which are highest volume
What a correct result looks like, and who decides that today
Which systems the result has to be written back into
What accuracy would have to be true before they trust it unattended

roles.partner: The client's examples, the integration work and the people who judge the output
roles.lyzr: The platform, the models and the engineer who sits with you through the proof

patterns.when: A packaged offer for a client the partner does not have yet. The audit is the way in, and it has to be worth paying for on its own.

first_offer.name: {work} audit
first_offer.ends_with: where the time actually goes in one {unit}, and a scoped build on the worst of it

delivery.shape: 6 week build on one {unit}, then recurring per {unit}
delivery.team_needed: 1 consultant who knows the domain + 1 engineer

patterns.expansion: The second {unit} is a shorter build, and the audit becomes the repeatable way in to the next client
discovery: How much of this work happens in a month, and who does it
Which parts are judgement and which are the same every time
What the output has to look like, and who signs it
What they have already tried here, and why it stopped

roles.partner: The domain expertise, the audit, the build and the client relationship
roles.lyzr: The platform, the templates to start from, and enablement for your team

patterns.when: The constraint is the environment rather than the workflow: regulated, sovereign, on-premise, or an architecture that has to be signed off before anything is built.

first_offer.name: {work} readiness review
first_offer.ends_with: what can run where, what the controls have to be, and a deployment plan their risk function can sign

delivery.shape: 10 to 12 week deployment on one {unit}, then infrastructure and support
delivery.team_needed: 1 solution architect + 1 infrastructure engineer + a compliance reviewer

patterns.expansion: A support and change contract on the environment, then the next workload into it
discovery: Where the data is allowed to live, and who decides that
What their risk or audit function has already asked about AI
Which environments are in scope, and who runs them
What has to be true before a decision can run without a person

roles.partner: The environment, the client's controls, the deployment and the ongoing support
roles.lyzr: The deployable platform, the governance layer and the architecture review

patterns.when: The client already has AI running that nobody owns. The money is in the control layer over it, not in building more.

first_offer.name: Agent estate assessment
first_offer.ends_with: an inventory of every agent and copilot running, what each one can reach, and a registry pilot

delivery.shape: 4 week discovery and registry, then an annual platform and advisory fee

patterns.expansion: An annual platform fee plus a quarterly review covering new agents as they are added
discovery: How many teams have deployed something, and on how many platforms
Whether anyone owns AI risk formally, and who they report to
What the audit or regulator has already asked for
Which environments and data the running agents can reach

roles.partner: The governance engagement, the risk relationship and the consultants who run it
roles.lyzr: OpenController for the registry and the controls, and the policy layer

patterns.when: Something is already live and fragile. The offer is to own it: monitoring, incidents, versions and a service level.

first_offer.name: {work} operations review
first_offer.ends_with: what is running, what is unmonitored, what has already broken, and a takeover plan

delivery.shape: Onboarding sprint to take it over, then a monthly fee per workload

patterns.expansion: The monthly fee grows with each new workload that goes live
discovery: What is running in production today, and who built it
Who gets called when it fails, and what their hours are
What has already gone wrong, and how they found out
What a service level would have to cover for them to sign

roles.partner: The support structure, the on-call rota and the client relationship
roles.lyzr: The platform, the observability and escalation into our engineering
